answers.core: It is a building block for add-ons.
answers.workaround:
We can choose to extend `ShaderMaterial` instead. The major downside is that in the editor `ShaderMaterial` will expose all the details of the shader and parameters which can be then arbitrarily modified. Users may get confused and accidentally break it. So it is better to have a dedicated empty base class to work with.

Extending `ShaderMaterial` is the current method I adopt. You can see from the below image that `ShaderMaterial` unnecessarily exposes all the shader parameters which are already presented by the top-level class. Not mention "private" parameters such as runtime LUTs (as they are provided by RID `ShaderMaterial` can't even show a value).

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/f723a861-fbd2-44fc-bc0c-7284b255598e)

2025-01-09: `ShaderMaterial` stores shaders and shader parameters in its resource. A custom material may not want it, as it may have better way to store them or generate them at runtime.
